name: Attention inequality
statement: Attention concentrates in a small tail: in one Twitter sample the top fifth of users held 97 percent of followers, and early success causes later success rather than only revealing it.
meaning: This names a shape in data rather than a mistake inside a head. Counts of followers, views, citations and downloads come out heavily skewed wherever they have been measured, so a small share of accounts or items absorbs most of what an audience has to give. Two separate claims travel under the one name. The first is descriptive: attention is concentrated, and the concentration can be summarised by a Gini coefficient or a Pareto share. The second is causal: the concentration is produced by cumulative advantage, in which having attention makes more attention easier to get, so an early lead compounds. The descriptive claim is arithmetic over a dataset and cannot be a judgement error, because no judgement is measured anywhere in it. The causal claim is about how a reward system behaves over time, not about how a person weighs evidence. Neither is a cognitive bias, and this entry is here to mark that rather than to dress a population statistic up as one. Robert Merton gave the causal version its usual name in 1968, the Matthew effect, and his subject was scientific credit rather than online audiences.

origin.note: The paper that puts the phrase in a title and measures the thing it names. It was posted on 26 January 2016 and carries an AAAI copyright line, and a Crossref search for its title and authors returns no journal or conference record, so the entry treats it as an unrefereed preprint. A Crossref bibliographic search for the phrase returns nothing earlier that uses it in this sense. The underlying regularity is much older. Merton's 1968 paper in Science, volume 159, issue 3810, pages 56 to 63, defines the Matthew effect as "the accruing of greater increments of recognition for particular scientific contributions to scientists of considerable repute and the withholding of such recognition from scientists who have not yet made their mark", and quotes the verse it is named for. Merton's evidence is interviews with Nobel laureates, one of whom told him the world "tends to give the credit to [already] famous people". No distribution is plotted in it.

evidence: Zhu and Lerman collected Twitter data from March to October 2014, starting from 5,600 randomly chosen seed users and following their friends, which produced 23,831,568 tweets and a dynamic network of 1,944,383 users and 17,869,415 edges. Across the seed users the Gini coefficient was 0.9412 for followers, 0.9133 for mentions and 0.9034 for retweets. Their introduction states that the top 20 percent of users own 97 percent of all followers, 93 percent of retweets and 93 percent of mentions; the abstract of the same paper says more than 96 percent for followers, and the entry quotes both because the paper does not reconcile them. Engagement is far less concentrated than attention: the Gini for the number of accounts a user follows is 0.6831, and for lifetime status updates 0.5939. Content shows the same shape as accounts. Cha, Kwak, Rodriguez, Ahn and Moon crawled the Entertainment and Science and Technology categories of YouTube alongside the Korean service Daum, and found the top 10 percent of videos taking nearly 80 percent of views. Their fits contradict the tidiest version of the story: the tail decays faster than a power law, and a power law with an exponential cutoff fits it better. The mechanism most often named for this is preferential attachment. Barabasi and Albert reported that the probability of a vertex having k links decays as a power law in several large networks. They give an exponent of 2.1 plus or minus 0.1 for the World Wide Web and 2.3 plus or minus 0.1 for a graph of 212,250 film actors. Their model, in which new vertices attach preferentially to well connected ones, gives 2.9 plus or minus 0.1. The nearest thing to a per-person judgement claim in this literature is about a person's own audience rather than about the distribution. Bernstein, Bakshy, Burke and Karrer surveyed active Facebook users, 542 in a general survey and 589 shown one of their own posts at least 48 hours old, and compared their guesses against server logs for 222,000 users over one month. For a specific post the median guess was 20 friends against a median actual audience of 78, which is 6 percent of a user's network guessed against 24 percent reached. The median relative error was 0.73, so the median estimate was 27 percent of the true audience. In the general survey the median guess was 50 against an actual 180, an underestimate by roughly a factor of three. That is a measured error in individual judgement, and its subject is how many people saw my post, not how attention is spread across everybody.

replication.headline: Independent datasets on different platforms keep producing the same concentration, and a regression discontinuity in grant funding shows early success causing later success. What repeats is a measurement, not an experiment on anyone's judgement.
replication.detail: The strongest test of the causal half is Bol, de Vaan and van de Rijt, who used the Netherlands Organization for Scientific Research's Innovation Research Incentives Scheme, which has concentrated 2,400,000,000 euros among 3,660 applicants since 2000. Funding runs on a hard threshold in evaluation scores, so applicants just above and just below it are comparable. Early career winners at ranks +1 and +2 were about two and a half times more likely to win a midcareer grant than nonwinners at ranks -1 and -2, exact test P < 0.001, with the win rate going from 10 to 26 percent. No other pair of neighbouring ranks differed. Publications, citations and h-index show no jump at the cutoff, before or after the competition, so the later advantage is not explained by work the grant paid for. Much of it is explained by nonwinners not applying again: the chance of submitting a midcareer proposal ran 40 percent below the threshold and 59 percent above it, exact test P < 0.001. After four years the lowest-ranked winners had received on average 40,000 euros more than the highest-ranked nonwinners, rank-sum test P < 0.01, growing to about 180,000 euros after eight years and more than twice as much grant money over the whole period. Van de Rijt, Kang, Restivo and Patil randomised arbitrary early success in four live systems covering funding, status, endorsement and reputation, and report in their abstract that recipients did better afterwards than untreated controls, with decreasing marginal returns and therefore a more modest role for cumulative advantage than had been assumed. Their abstract was read at Europe PMC. What does not replicate is the form of the distribution. Broido and Clauset fitted 928 network data sets from the Index of Complex Networks and classified each by how much evidence it gives for scale-free structure. Forty-nine percent fall into their Not Scale Free category, 29 percent meet the weakest criterion that a power law is a plausible model of some part of the upper tail, and 10 and 4 percent meet their Strong and Strongest criteria. In 88 percent of networks a log-normal fits the degrees as well as or better than a power law, and they report social networks as at best weakly scale free.

study.cite: Bol, T., de Vaan, M., & van de Rijt, A. (2018). The Matthew effect in science funding. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 115(19), 4887-4890.

limits: A Gini coefficient is a property of a metric and a population, not of a platform, and it moves a long way when either changes. Zhu and Lerman's own figures make the point: 0.9412 for followers against 0.5939 for posting activity, in the same sample of the same people. Their sample is 5,600 seed users drawn from a numeric id range on one service in 2014, and the paper is a preprint. Concentration on its own settles nothing about cause. A skewed distribution is equally consistent with cumulative advantage and with talent being skewed, which is why the regression discontinuity and the randomised interventions carry the causal weight here and the Gini coefficients carry none of it. Both of those run in reward systems with formal applications and thresholds, and neither is about audiences on a feed. No experiment measuring an individual's judgement about how attention is distributed was located. Searching covered Crossref bibliographic queries for the phrase and for its authors, Semantic Scholar's record for the 2001 study named below, Europe PMC, and web searches pairing the phrase with bias, judgement, experiment and definition. The closest candidate found is Zuckerman and Jost's survey of self-rated popularity against network position, in Social Psychology Quarterly for September 2001, volume 64, issue 3, pages 207 to 223. It is paywalled at the publisher and at JSTOR, no copy of its text or abstract could be opened, and nothing it reports is quoted here. This site treats the popularity signal itself in the bandwagon effect entry and the sequential-choice model in the information cascade entry.
misreadings: The first misreading is filing this as a bias at all. It appears on bias lists beside the anchoring effect, and a Lorenz curve over follower counts is a different kind of object from an experiment in which people give a wrong answer. Nothing in the descriptive literature identifies a person, a judgement or a normative standard the judgement fell short of. The second is the folklore that most published papers are never cited. Lariviere, Gingras and Archambault tracked citations to more than 27 million papers indexed in the Web of Science between 1900 and 2007. In 2005, with a two-year window, citations reached 80 percent of papers in medical fields, 60 percent in natural sciences and engineering and 55 percent in the social sciences. With a five-year window ending in 2002, only 12, 27 and 32 percent respectively remained uncited. Concentration has been falling, not rising: the share of papers accounting for 80 percent of citations grew from 24 to 33 percent in medicine and from 23 to 28 percent in natural sciences and engineering between 1990 and 2005. The humanities behave differently, with 7.2 percent of papers taking 80 percent of citations in 2005. Their paper was written against Evans, whose abstract reports that as more journal issues came online, fewer journals and articles were cited and more of those citations went to fewer of them, over a database of 34 million articles. That Evans measured concentration with the Herfindahl-Hirschman index alone is Lariviere and colleagues' description of him, not something read in his paper. So the direction of the trend in science is contested even where the level is not. A third misreading treats heavy concentration as proof of a power law, and through it of preferential attachment. Cha and colleagues found a cutoff in the tail on YouTube, Broido and Clauset found log-normal fits doing as well or better in 88 percent of 928 networks, and concentration survives all of that untouched. The last one runs the causal claim too hard. Van de Rijt and colleagues, who created early advantage at random, report decreasing marginal returns and read their own result as a smaller role for cumulative advantage than had been supposed.

sources.text: Zhu, L., & Lerman, K. (2016). Attention inequality in social media. arXiv:1601.07200. Full text read from the PDF for the Gini coefficients, the top-20-percent shares, the sample sizes and the collection dates. No journal or conference version is recorded in Crossref.
Merton, R. K. (1968). The Matthew effect in science. Science, 159(3810), 56-63. Read from the scanned copy linked here for the definition and the laureate's quotation.

Barabasi, A.-L., & Albert, R. (1999). Emergence of scaling in random networks. Science, 286(5439), 509-512. Read from the arXiv version cond-mat/9910332 for the exponents and the preferential attachment model.

Cha, M., Kwak, H., Rodriguez, P., Ahn, Y.-Y., & Moon, S. (2007). I tube, you tube, everybody tubes. Proceedings of the 7th ACM SIGCOMM Internet Measurement Conference, 1-14. Full text read for the 10 percent to 80 percent result and the truncated tail.

Bol, T., de Vaan, M., & van de Rijt, A. (2018). The Matthew effect in science funding. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 115(19), 4887-4890. Full text read at PubMed Central for the regression discontinuity, the percentages and the euro figures.

van de Rijt, A., Kang, S. M., Restivo, M., & Patil, A. (2014). Field experiments of success-breeds-success dynamics. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 111(19), 6934-6939. Abstract read through the Europe PMC REST service, linked here; the full text was not opened, and only the abstract is used.
Broido, A. D., & Clauset, A. (2019). Scale-free networks are rare. Nature Communications, 10, 1017. Full text read for the 928 data sets, the category percentages and the log-normal comparison.

Lariviere, V., Gingras, Y., & Archambault, E. (2009). The decline in the concentration of citations, 1900-2007. Journal of the American Society for Information Science and Technology, 60(4), 858-862. Figures read from the authors' arXiv copy 0809.5250, linked here.

Evans, J. A. (2008). Electronic publication and the narrowing of science and scholarship. Science, 321(5887), 395-399. Abstract read through the Europe PMC REST service, linked here; the publisher's full text is paywalled and the Herfindahl figures were not read.

Bernstein, M. S., Bakshy, E., Burke, M., & Karrer, B. (2013). Quantifying the invisible audience in social networks. Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, 21-30. Full text read for the survey sizes, the medians and the 27 percent relative error.

Zuckerman, E. W., & Jost, J. T. (2001). What makes you think you're so popular? Self-evaluation maintenance and the subjective side of the friendship paradox. Social Psychology Quarterly, 64(3), 207-223. Named because it is the closest located candidate for a per-person judgement study. Bibliographic details verified at Crossref and ProQuest; the text and abstract are paywalled and were not read, and nothing is quoted from it.
